source.title: Prediction of Anaerobic Power From Standing Long Jump in NCAA Division IA Football Players

paper.citation: Mann J.B., Bird M., Signorile J.F., Brechue W.F., Mayhew J.L. Prediction of Anaerobic Power From Standing Long Jump in NCAA Division IA Football Players. Journal of Strength & Conditioning Research. 2021;35(6):1542-1546. doi:10.1519/JSC.0000000000004043.
paper.abstract: This paper addresses the following question: Can standing long jump distance and anthropometric measurements estimate force-plate-derived peak and average horizontal power in NCAA Division I football players? Fifty-eight adult players from one NCAA Division IA American-football program were tested after a 10-week winter conditioning program. Standing long jump was already part of their routine evaluation, so the athletes were familiar with the task. This was a single-cohort, cross-sectional prediction study. After warm-up and familiarization, players completed two maximal standing long jumps from a three-dimensional force plate sampled at 1,000 Hz.
paper.tldr: Standing-long-jump distance and peak power were highly reliable between trials, with ICCs of 0.944 and 0.926, respectively. The peak-power equation was: power in watts = 32.49 × jump distance in centimeters + 39.69 × body mass in kilograms − 7,608; model R was 0.86, standard error of estimate was 488 W, and CV was 9.3%. The equation can provide a practical estimate when body mass and a standardized standing long jump are available, but the raw jump distance remains the directly observed measurement and may be more stable for longitudinal monitoring.
paper.methods: This was a single-cohort, cross-sectional prediction study. After warm-up and familiarization, players completed two maximal standing long jumps from a three-dimensional force plate sampled at 1,000 Hz. Jump distance, body mass, height, and leg segment lengths were evaluated as predictors. Stepwise regression selected predictors, and random 70%/30% subsamples were used for internal cross-validation.
paper.findings: Standing-long-jump distance and peak power were highly reliable between trials, with ICCs of 0.944 and 0.926, respectively. The peak-power equation was: power in watts = 32.49 × jump distance in centimeters + 39.69 × body mass in kilograms − 7,608; model R was 0.86, standard error of estimate was 488 W, and CV was 9.3%. Jump distance contributed 56.8% and body mass 43.2% of the explained peak-power variance; leg lengths and ratios did not add significantly. Internal split-sample correlations between predicted and measured peak power were 0.83 in the 70% subset and 0.70 in the 30% subset. The estimated smallest worthwhile changes were 10.4 cm for jump distance and 632 W for peak power, emphasizing that small observed changes may be measurement noise.
paper.limitations: The equation was derived from 58 experienced adult male athletes in one Division I program at one time point. The 70%/30% procedure was internal split-sample checking, not external validation in a new team, season, testing surface, or device. Stepwise selection can be sample-sensitive, and the peak-power standard error of 488 W is material for individual interpretation. The equation estimates the specific force-plate power outcome used here; it does not establish anaerobic capacity, sprint ability, game performance, or training causality.
paper.practicalImplications: The equation can provide a practical estimate when body mass and a standardized standing long jump are available, but the raw jump distance remains the directly observed measurement and may be more stable for longitudinal monitoring. Keep technique, warm-up, surface, footwear, and landing rules consistent. Interpret predicted power alongside the 488-W error and the study's change thresholds. Before using the equation for selection, return-to-play, or position norms, locally compare estimates against force-plate data and assess bias across position and body-mass groups.
paper.athleteDev: For athlete development, the equation can provide a practical estimate when body mass and a standardized standing long jump are available, but the raw jump distance remains the directly observed measurement and may be more stable for longitudinal monitoring. Keep technique, warm-up, surface, footwear, and landing rules consistent. Interpret predicted power alongside the 488-W error and the study's change thresholds. Before using the equation for selection, return-to-play, or position norms, locally compare estimates against force-plate data and assess bias across position and body-mass groups. Apply the finding within the population and setting described in the source rather than treating it as a universal threshold.
paper.rtp: The paper did not validate a rehabilitation or return-to-sport decision rule. Its findings may inform supporting training or monitoring during reconditioning, but it provides no standalone clearance threshold or progression criterion.
